findings.explanation: The module exposes two overlapping IAM mechanisms on the same repository. var.iam_bindings drives google_sourcerepo_repository_iam_member.binding (additive, per role/member), while var.repository_readers drives google_sourcerepo_repository_iam_binding.readers (authoritative for roles/source.reader). var.iam_bindings is required (its validation demands at least one entry) and the example passes roles/source.reader through it, so the collision sits on the default path, not an edge case. If a consumer populates repository_readers AND keeps roles/source.reader in iam_bindings, the authoritative binding overwrites the role's member list on every apply and the additive member re-adds itself on the next one: a permanent diff, with whichever ran last silently deciding who actually has read access.
findings.remediation: Reject the overlap at plan time rather than discovering it at apply time. Add a lifecycle precondition to the authoritative binding asserting that roles/source.reader is not also present in var.iam_bindings.
findings.title: Authoritative and additive IAM resources can both manage roles/source.reader, causing permanent apply thrash

findings.explanation: google_sourcerepo_repository.pike publishes commit notifications into google_pubsub_topic.pike via pubsub_configs, but neither the module nor example/examplea creates a google_pubsub_subscription. With no subscription attached there is no delivery path at all, so every notification the repository emits expires unread after the 7-day topic retention. holden's HLD_GCP_281 enforces this same invariant, but only for topics used as dead-letter targets, so this configuration passes the deterministic scan.
findings.remediation: Either document that consumers must attach their own subscription to the exported topic, or ship an optional subscription in the module gated on a variable. The topic is already exported via output "topic", so a consumer-owned subscription is viable; the gap is that nothing states this is required for the notifications to be useful.
findings.title: Repository notification topic has no subscription, so Cloud Source Repository events are discarded
findings.verification: Optional pull subscription plus dead-letter topic, DLQ subscription and the two service-agent grants, all gated on var.create_subscription (default false). Enabled in example/examplea. HLD_GCP_120/121/122/280/281/460/461/464 all pass; HLD_GCP_121 on the DLQ subscription itself is suppressed in source as structurally unfixable.

findings.explanation: The description reads "Key for Pub/Sub access", which suggests an access credential. The value is assigned to google_pubsub_topic.kms_key_name and must be a fully-qualified Cloud KMS crypto key resource ID. The example passes google_kms_crypto_key.cloudsource.id, but a consumer reading only the README variable table cannot infer the required format, and a wrong value fails at apply rather than plan.
findings.remediation: State the expected KMS resource ID in the description and tighten the validation from a non-empty check to a format check.
findings.title: var.key description does not say it must be a KMS crypto key ID

findings.explanation: message_retention_duration = "604800s" is the maximum Pub/Sub allows and is baked into the module. Topic-level retention is billed storage, so a consumer that only needs an hour of replay pays for seven days and cannot opt out without forking the module. Every other tunable on this module is a variable; this one is not.
findings.remediation: Promote the value to a variable with the current 604800s as the default, preserving behaviour for existing consumers.
findings.title: Topic message retention is hardcoded to 7 days with no way for a consumer to change it

findings.explanation: The file's entire content is '# required'. It is not required: Terraform loads every .tf file in the directory, and this module already splits resources into one file per resource type. It is a leftover from a scaffold and misleads anyone opening it looking for the module entry point.
findings.title: main.tf is an empty placeholder containing only a comment

findings.explanation: The valid, compare and planned targets invoke checkov, and two pass --external-checks-dir ../../checkov. The repo has deleted .checkov.yml and replaced the checkov pre-commit hook with holden, and no ../../checkov directory exists, so these targets now fail or silently no-op (two are prefixed with - to ignore errors). Anyone running 'make valid' gets a false all-clear that no longer matches what pre-commit and CI enforce.
findings.remediation: Replace the checkov invocations in the valid, compare and planned targets with 'holden scan .' so the example's local verification matches the enforced gate.
findings.title: Example Makefile still drives checkov after the repo migrated to holden
findings.verification: checkov/terrascan/tfsec/kics targets removed by the user; a valid target running terraform fmt, terraform validate and holden scan ../.. was restored, since validate.sh and validate.ps1 both invoke make valid and were broken by the removal. Verified: make valid reports 0 failed / 210 passed.
